say.en: sin 30 degrees, sin 150 degrees and sin 390 degrees are all 1 over 2. If we ask "which angle has sine one half?", we must agree on one answer. That agreement is the principal value. In this lesson: Restrict sine and cosine to make them one-one.
State the domain and range of sin to the power minus 1 and cos to the power minus 1.
Find principal values.

body.en: sin is not one-one on $R$: $\sin 0 = \sin \pi = 0$. On $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ it is one-one and takes every value in $[-1, 1]$, so it has an *inverse* there: $\sin^{-1} : [-1, 1] \to [-\pi/2, \pi/2]$. This interval is the principal value branch.
body.kn: R ಮೇಲೆ sin ಏಕೈಕವಲ್ಲ. [−π/2, π/2] ನಲ್ಲಿ ಅದು ಏಕೈಕ ಮತ್ತು [−1, 1] ನ ಎಲ್ಲ ಬೆಲೆಗಳನ್ನು ಪಡೆಯುತ್ತದೆ. ಆದ್ದರಿಂದ sin⁻¹ : [−1, 1] → [−π/2, π/2]. ಇದೇ ಮುಖ್ಯ ಬೆಲೆಯ ಶಾಖೆ.

title.en: Cutting sine down to an invertible piece

say.en: Sine repeats, so a horizontal line cuts it many times: it is not one-one on R. Keep only the yellow piece from minus pi by 2 to pi by 2.
Swap the roles of x and y. The yellow piece, reflected in y equals x, is the graph of sine inverse.
Cosine is one-one on zero to pi instead, so cos inverse takes values from zero to pi.
Two quick values. Sine inverse of one half is pi by 6. Cos inverse of minus one half is pi minus pi by 3, that is 2 pi by 3.

say.en: Let us solve this together. Find the principal value of sin to the power minus 1(1/ the square root of 2) and cos to the power minus 1(minus 1 over 2).
sin(pi /4) equals 1/ the square root of 2 and pi /4 in [- pi /2, pi /2], so sin to the power minus 1(1/ the square root of 2) equals pi /4.
cos(pi /3) equals 1 over 2, so cos(pi - pi /3) equals minus 1 over 2.
2 pi /3 in [0, pi ], so cos to the power minus 1(minus 1 over 2) equals 2 pi /3.
So the answer is pi /4 and 2 pi /3.
